title: Unto the mountains (Psalm 121)
hookLine: "He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep"
last: MORE THAN WATCHMEN FOR THE MORNING.

cards: In some Jewish homes, a small printed card hangs near a newborn's crib. Others keep the same words folded in a wallet for a long drive, or tucked into a suitcase.
Eight short verses, turning on one plain fact about people: sooner or later, guards doze and parents nod off. Nobody can keep watch forever. The psalm on the card says there is a keeper who can.
It starts with a traveler looking up at the hills.

teach.b: It's another Song of Ascents, often read as a pilgrim's song. A traveler on the road to Jerusalem looks up at the hills ahead. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: from whence shall my help come?"
Some readers hear worry in the question: hills are where danger can hide on a long road.

teach.h: HELP FROM THE MAKER OF HEAVEN.
teach.b: The answer comes straight back: my help comes from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth. Not from the mountains; from the One who made them.
Then the great promise: "Behold, He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep."
The Hebrew word is shomer: a keeper, a guard, someone who stays alert while others rest. In just eight verses, forms of that word appear six times. The Lord is your keeper.
He'll keep you from all evil, keep your going out and your coming in, from now and forever. The sun won't strike you by day, nor the moon by night.
That's why many Jews say this psalm for protection: before a journey, for a woman giving birth, at a sickbed. Hasidic teachers found a hidden reading in the opening question.
From where, me-ayin, can also be heard as from ayin, from nothingness.
In that reading, help begins the moment a person admits there is nothing left. And under it stands the psalm's promise: a keeper who stays awake when you can't.

how: Many Jews recite Psalm 121 before travel, at a sickbed and for protection in childbirth; it is often printed on cards or plaques placed near a newborn, and it is part of the Shabbat afternoon psalms in some communities.

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the psalm says help comes from the mountains
help comes from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth.
the word for keeper appears again and again in Psalm 121

games.q: you're a pilgrim on the road, looking up at hills where danger might hide. you ask: where will my help come from? what does the psalm answer?
o: from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth.
games.why: my help comes from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth. the keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps.

practice: Look at a hill, a skyline or the edge of the sky, or close your eyes and picture mountains far off, and notice how different it feels to look up and out instead of down.
Ask the psalm's question quietly, where will my help come from, and picture the people you watch over kept, even while you sleep. If you pray, say the psalm's promise.

wordCard.voice: Shomer. A keeper, a guard, one who stays alert while others rest — the word Psalm one twenty-one uses six times for the One who neither slumbers nor sleeps.

orig.note: Hebrew: keeper of Israel, from Psalm 121:4.

carryVoice: Your line: he doesn't sleep. Someone else can hold the night shift. That's day three hundred twenty-five.
